note: Changed from existing draft 'balam' (colonial/Classic spelling) to show the long vowel of modern Yucatec, written báalam with tone in Bricker et al. 1998 and Bastarrachea et al. Diccionario básico. Alternative: chak mo'ol (also cited for jaguar/puma; regional). Association: balamo'ob are also guardian spirits of milpa and village in traditional belief; the animal sense is ordinary everyday usage, but reviewers should confirm it reads as the animal for children.
Kept existing draft. Widely documented (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico; Cordemex). Tone/length marking varies across sources (ts'unu'un vs ts'úunu'un).

review_question: For the Andean llama, do you use a Maya word or just say 'llama'? How do you pronounce it?
note: Spanish loanword. The llama is Andean and not native to the peninsula; no traditional Yucatec word is expected. Medium only because it is clearly a loan; Spanish spelling kept per loan policy; pronunciation may be [jama]. Do not invent a native term. Alternative to review: keep Spanish spelling as a marked loan.

review_question: Do you have any word for the condor, or would you say 'cóndor' (or something like nojoch ch'oom, 'big vulture')?
note: Spanish loan (cóndor), kept in Spanish spelling per loan policy. Andean bird, not native to the region. Alternative descriptive: nojoch ch'oom 'big vulture' (nojoch 'big' + ch'oom 'vulture/zopilote', both attested), which is transparent but not an established name.
Standard word, written péepem with tone (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico). Also used for moths.

úulum = domestic turkey (Bricker et al. 1998; Cordemex ulum). The wild ocellated turkey of the peninsula is kuuts, a different bird; the card shows the gobbling domestic turkey. Association: turkeys are offered in some traditional ceremonies; the word itself is everyday.

review_question: How do you say 'turtle': áak, aak, or ak? Is the vowel long? Could a child confuse it with áaktun (cave) or p'aak (tomato) when called aloud?
note: áak 'turtle' (Cordemex; Bricker et al. 1998). Risk: near-homophones on this deck (aaktun cave, p'aak tomato) and elsewhere (ak' 'vine'); reviewers should confirm vowel length and the plain vs ejective k. Species names exist for sea vs land turtles; this is the general term. IPA ?.

review_question: Is 'much' only a toad, or also a green frog like this picture? What do you call a green frog? Is wo' fine for children or tied to the rain ceremony?
note: much is the common word for toad, used loosely for frogs (Diccionario básico; Bricker); it may not cover the green frog of the card, hence low. wo' (uo), a rain-singing frog, is avoided as the card word because wo' frogs are part of the Ch'a' Cháak rain ceremony, where children imitate their calls.
kàan/káan 'snake' (Bricker et al. 1998). Do not confuse with ka'an 'sky' (glottal stop) or kaan 'four' in some spellings. Association: the feathered serpent K'uk'ulkan; the plain word is everyday.
Kept existing draft. Standard word for maize grain (all major dictionaries). Related: nal 'ear of corn (fresh)'. Maize carries deep cultural and ritual weight, but ixi'im is the ordinary noun.

review_question: How do you say 'nopal': pak'am or pak'an? Is it used for the plant, the fruit (tuna), or both?
note: pak'am (also pak'an) 'nopal, tuna' in Cordemex and Diccionario básico. Final m vs n varies by source; reviewers should confirm. Opuntia occurs on the peninsula but is less culturally central than in central Mexico. IPA ?.
Kept existing draft. Standard word (all major dictionaries). Specific varieties have their own names (e.g. ib 'lima bean').

review_question: Is there a Maya word for pineapple, or do people just say 'piña'?
note: Spanish loanword. I could not confirm a native Yucatec name for pineapple from sources I trust; rather than guess, this is left as a marked loan. Colonial dictionaries may record a native term; a reviewer should check Cordemex. Spanish spelling kept per loan policy.

ìik/iik 'chile' (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico), as in x-ma'ax iik. Minimal pair with iik' 'wind' (ejective k') on the viento card; callers must pronounce the ejective clearly, and reviewers may want to flag this pair for children.

review_question: Do people say 'papa' for potato in Maya, or another word?
note: Spanish loanword. Potato is Andean; no traditional Yucatec name expected. Do not substitute iis, which is sweet potato (camote), a different plant.
óon 'avocado' (Bricker et al. 1998; Cordemex on). Short, may need a clear call.
p'aak 'tomato' (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico). Native word.

review_question: What do you call a sunflower? Would 'u lool k'iin' sound natural, strange, or wrong?
note: Built from attested roots: u (3rd person possessive) + lool 'flower' + k'iin 'sun'. Not an established name. Sunflower is not a traditional peninsular crop; speakers most likely say girasol (Spanish loan), which is a safe alternative. The possessive phrase order should be checked by a speaker. IPA ?.
Kept existing draft. k'iin = sun, day, time (all major dictionaries). Association: K'inich, solar deity; the plain noun is everyday. Respectful address forms (e.g. Yuum K'iin) avoided.
Kept existing draft. uj = moon, month (all major dictionaries). Some speakers use respectful/ritual address forms for the moon; those are avoided here.
éek' 'star' (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico). Do not confuse with ek' 'black, dark' in some colonial spellings.

review_question: What is the everyday word for 'rain' (the noun): ja'al, ja'ajal, cháak, or something else? Is cháak acceptable for children, or only for the rain deity?
note: Changed from ja'ajal (reviewer flagged it unverified; it may be the verb 'to rain'). ja'al is offered as the noun 'rain', derived from ja' 'water'; IPA ? and form unverified. Deliberately avoided: cháak, which can mean rain in everyday speech but is also the name of the rain deity (Ch'a' Cháak ceremony); if speakers say cháak for rain the owner must decide whether that is acceptable.

review_question: What do you call a lightning flash in everyday speech? Is 'lelem' right, and is the word connected to the Chaako'ob in a way that should stay off a children's game?
note: lelem 'lightning, flash' as I recall it from Cordemex (cf. lemba' 'to shine'); kept as attested only on that recollection, with low confidence: I cannot confirm it is the everyday modern word. IPA ?. Association: lightning is tied to the Chaako'ob (rain deities) and their axes; avoid any form naming them.

review_question: What do you call a rainbow? Is 'chéel' right? Is the rainbow considered dangerous or unlucky, and would it be OK on a children's card?
note: PROVISIONAL. chéel 'rainbow' as recalled from Cordemex/Bricker; I am not sure of the form or that it is in everyday use, so confidence is low. Taboo risk: in some communities the rainbow is considered dangerous (said to come out of cenotes, cause illness, not to be pointed at), and it is linked in scholarship with Ix Chel. A speaker must confirm it is acceptable on a children's card.
múuyal 'cloud' (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico).
iik' 'wind, breath' (all major dictionaries). Also means spirit/breath and is a day name in the calendar; the everyday sense is wind. Minimal pair with iik 'chile' (plain k) on the chile card.

review_question: Is there a Maya word for a comet? Would 'búuts' éek'' (smoke star) be understood, or do people say 'cometa'?
note: búuts' 'smoke' (long vowel, as in Bricker et al. 1998) + éek' 'star'. Earlier draft wrote short buts'. I believe colonial dictionaries record budz ek for comet, which would make it attested, but I have not verified it, so it is descriptive, low. Alternative: Spanish loan cometa.

review_question: Is 'wits' the word for a big mountain, or only for a hill? Would you use puuk?
note: wits (colonial witz) 'hill, mountain' (Cordemex; Bricker). The peninsula is flat; locally the word mostly names hills. Alternative: puuk 'range of hills' (the Puuc). Snowy peaks in the verse have no local referent.

review_question: How would you say 'volcano'? Would 'k'aak'il wits' (fire mountain) make sense, or do people just say 'volcán'?
note: Built from k'aak' 'fire' + -il (relational suffix) + wits 'hill/mountain'. There are no volcanoes on the peninsula and no traditional word is expected; Spanish volcán is the likely everyday form and a safe alternative. Modifier construction needs a speaker's check (k'aak' wits vs k'aak'il wits). IPA ?.

review_question: What do you call a spring where water comes out of the ground? Is 'sayab' a word you know or use?
note: sayab 'manantial, ojo de agua' (Cordemex). Its everyday modern use is uncertain. Alternative culturally central water source: ts'ono'ot 'cenote', but that is a sinkhole, a different referent, and cenotes have strong ritual associations; not used. Lowered to low: I recall sayab from Cordemex but not its modern currency.
k'áak'nab 'sea' (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico).

review_question: How would you say 'desert'? Would 'tikin lu'um' (dry land) make sense, or do people say 'desierto'?
note: tikin 'dry' + lu'um 'earth, land', both attested. No deserts on the peninsula; not an established term. Spanish desierto is a likely everyday alternative. IPA ?.
k'áax 'forest, wild land, monte' (all major dictionaries). Covers scrub forest broadly, not only tall jungle. The verse's monkeys fit (ma'ax 'spider monkey').

review_question: Do you say 'cristal' for a rock crystal? Is there a Maya word that is NOT the sáastun of the j-meen?
note: Spanish loan, kept in Spanish spelling per loan policy. Deliberately avoided: sáastun 'clear stone', the divining crystal used by the j-meen (traditional ritual specialist), a sacred object. Also avoided sáasil tuunich 'clear stone' for being too close to it.

review_question: Do people today say 'peten' for an island, or mostly 'isla'?
note: peten 'island' (Cordemex; source of the place name Petén). Well attested historically; reviewers should confirm current everyday use versus Spanish isla.

áaktun (colonial actun) 'cave' (Bricker et al. 1998; Cordemex). Association: caves are traditional offering places and entrances to the underworld in belief; the noun itself is everyday (common in place names).

review_question: What do you call a clay cooking pot: kum or kuum? Is it different from p'uul?
note: kum/kuum 'olla' (Cordemex; Diccionario básico). Vowel length uncertain across sources. Related: p'uul 'water jar (cántaro)', a different vessel. IPA ?.

review_question: What do you call a woven basket: xúuxak, xak, or something else? Is the vowel long?
note: Kept xúuxak over xak: my recollection is that xúuxak is the modern basket word and xak the colonial form (Cordemex xac), but I am not sure; low. Length ?. IPA ?.

review_question: What do you call a drum like this one (hit with hands or sticks)? Is 'tunkul' / 'tunk'ul' that drum, or only the hollow log drum? Is it tied to ceremonies?
note: tunkul / tunk'ul (colonial spelling tunkul) is the hollow-log slit drum (cf. Nahuatl teponaztli). Uncertain: plain vs ejective k, and whether it fits a hand drum. The skin drum is pax/paax in some sources, but paax now commonly means 'music'. Association: used in traditional ceremonies and dances. IPA ?.

review_question: Is there a Maya word for a mud brick, or do people say 'adobe'?
note: Spanish loan. Adobe is not a traditional peninsular building material (houses are stone, bajareque/wattle-and-daub, and palm thatch), so no native term is expected. Descriptive alternative for review: luk' tuunich 'mud stone' (luk' 'mud' + tuunich 'stone'), not established.

review_question: What do you call cotton thread: k'u'uch, k'uuch, or something else?
note: k'u'uch 'thread, spun cotton' (Bricker et al. 1998; Cordemex). Related: piits' 'cotton' (raw). Glottal placement needs confirmation. Lowered to low: form and glottal placement unverified. IPA ?.

review_question: Do people still say 'chem' for a canoe or small boat?
note: chem 'canoe, boat' (Cordemex; Bricker). Well attested historically; reviewers should confirm everyday use (some speakers may say barco or kanoa for boats).

review_question: Is there a Maya word for a bridge, or do people say 'puente'?
note: Spanish loan, likely the everyday form in a region with few rivers. I could not confirm a native everyday word. Colonial dictionaries may record a term (to check in Cordemex). Do not invent one.
kib 'wax, candle' (all major dictionaries). Association: candles are central to offerings (e.g. Janal Pixan, Day of the Dead) but the word is everyday.

review_question: Is there a Maya word for a hammer, or do people say 'martillo'?
note: Spanish loan, kept in Spanish spelling per loan policy (earlier draft respelling 'martiyo' removed as unsourced). Related native verb: baj 'to hammer, nail in' (Bricker), but I do not know a native tool noun.
naj/naaj 'house' (all major dictionaries; length varies by source). Alternative: otoch 'home', usually possessed (in wotoch 'my home').
kool 'milpa' (all major dictionaries). Spanish milpa is not from Maya (it is from Nahuatl). Association: milpa ceremonies (e.g. jaanli kool) exist but kool itself is ordinary.

review_question: What do you call the corner shop: 'tienda', 'kúuchil koonol', or something else?
note: kúuchil 'place' + koonol 'selling' (kon 'to sell'), both attested. Transparent phrase, not confirmed as the usual word; many speakers likely say tienda (Spanish loan), a safe alternative. IPA ?.

review_question: What do you call the town square: k'íiwik, or 'plaza'? Long vowel?
note: k'íiwik (colonial kiuic) 'plaza, market' (Cordemex; Bricker). Vowel length and ejective need confirmation. IPA ?.

review_question: Is there a Maya word for a harbour, or do people say 'puerto'?
note: Spanish loan, likely the everyday form (cf. place names Puerto Progreso, Puerto Morelos). Descriptive alternative for review: u kúuchil chem 'place of the canoes' (kúuchil 'place' + chem 'canoe'), not established.
kaaj/kaj 'town, community' (all major dictionaries; Restall's work on the colonial cah). Length varies by source.

review_question: Do people say 'escuela' in Maya, or 'najil xook' / another phrase?
note: Changed from descriptive naajil xook. I believe speakers mostly say escuela, and naajil xook is too close to naaj (casa) for a three-choice call. Alternative for review: naajil xook 'house of reading/study' (naaj 'house' + -il + xook 'read, study'), which I believe appears in bilingual-education materials but cannot cite.

review_question: Do people say 'observatorio', or is there a Maya way to say 'a place to watch the stars'?
note: Spanish loan; modern institution with no traditional word. Kept as loan (not a naajil- phrase, to avoid clashing with naaj on casa). Descriptive alternative for review: naajil u cha'anta'al eek'o'ob 'house where the stars are watched' (cha'an 'to watch', eek' 'star', -o'ob plural), grammar unverified. Note El Caracol at Chichén Itzá is popularly called an observatory, but that name is Spanish.

review_question: Do people say 'biblioteca', or a phrase like 'najil ju'un'?
note: Changed from descriptive naajil ju'un. Modern institution; Spanish biblioteca is the likely everyday form, and the naajil- phrase clashed with naaj (casa). Alternative for review: naajil ju'un 'house of paper/books' (naaj + -il + ju'un 'paper, book'), not established, no institutional source.
